title: Priority Boarding in Lift Group Control: A Simulation Study of Its Cost to Other Passengers and of a Priority-Aware Destination Control Rule
content: Passengers with access requirements, such as wheelchair users, may be given priority when boarding a lift. This study quantifies what such a policy costs other passengers and tests whether destination control can honour it. An open discrete-event lift simulator is verified by automated tests and agrees with the classical up-peak round-trip time within 2%. Five group controllers, two boarding rules and two priority-passenger profiles are compared in 31,680 paired runs under steady and time-varying demand. Every measured passenger is followed for at least 900 s, so a mean waiting time restricted to 600 s is observed exactly for all arrivals. With landing-call control, priority-first boarding raises other passengers’ restricted mean wait by at most 3.3 s in any cell below the reference demand (the up-peak handling capacity); at the reference demand it adds 1.8 s (95% interval 1.3 to 2.4) and saves priority passengers 9.3 s (8.0 to 10.7). Under destination control, priority at the door has no measurable effect up to the reference demand, because each passenger may board only the allocated car. A priority-aware allocation rule (DCS-P0) reduces priority passengers’ wait by 30% to 43% there while adding 0.6 to 4.1 s for others, but under sustained overload it raises the all-passenger mean by 29.9 s. Passengers who need more space reduce capacity for everyone by more than boarding order changes any wait. Priority boarding is thus inexpensive in normal operation, but under destination control the priority label must enter car allocation.
